name: Authorization
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Being Known Is Not the Same as Being Allowed
lesson.summary: Authorization is the separate step of deciding what an already-authenticated identity is permitted to do, and conflating it with authentication is one of the most common security design mistakes.
lesson.body:
Authentication, from the previous chapter, answers "who are you?" Authorization is a completely separate question that only makes sense to ask afterward: "what are you allowed to do?" It is tempting to treat these as one step, especially in small systems where every logged-in user can do everything, but the distinction becomes unavoidable the moment a system has more than one kind of user or more than one kind of action. A hospital's records system might authenticate a nurse and a billing clerk through the identical login process, yet authorize the nurse to view patient charts while authorizing the clerk only to view invoices. Same authentication mechanism, entirely different authorization outcomes.

Traditional systems implement authorization through mechanisms like access control lists, which attach a list of permitted identities and actions directly to a resource, or role-based access control, which groups permissions into named roles, such as admin, editor, or viewer, and assigns identities to roles rather than managing individual permissions one by one. Either way, the pattern is the same: authentication happens once to establish identity, and then every subsequent action is checked against a separate set of rules that determines whether that specific identity may perform that specific action on that specific resource.

Blockchains enforce authorization in a notably different, almost accidental way, and it is worth pausing on because it clarifies the general concept well. There is no central administrator checking a permissions table before approving a transaction. Instead, the protocol's own rules make unauthorized actions mathematically impossible to execute successfully. Alice authenticates herself as the controller of an address by producing a valid signature with the matching private key, exactly as described earlier. But that signature only authorizes her to spend the specific funds recorded as belonging to that address. If Alice tries to construct a transaction spending coins from Bob's address, no signature she produces with her own key will verify against Bob's public key, so the network's nodes simply reject the transaction outright. Authorization here is not a permissions list somebody checks, it is baked directly into what the cryptography will and will not allow to succeed.

This distinction matters well beyond blockchains, because conflating authentication with authorization is a recurring source of real security failures. A system that only checks "is this a logged-in user?" before allowing an action, without separately checking "is this particular logged-in user allowed to do this particular thing?", is vulnerable to any authenticated user reaching into data or actions meant for someone else entirely, a bug category sometimes called broken access control. Keeping the two questions conceptually and architecturally separate, proving identity first, then checking permission against that identity second, is one of the more boring but consistently important lessons in security design.
